media.title: Qutub Minar: Drawing the Line of Sight Step by Step
media.description: An animated introduction to the line of sight concept, anchored in the Qutub Minar scenario. The animation shows an observer figure near the minaret, traces the oblique line of sight from the observer's eye to the minaret tip, then transitions to a coordinate diagram where vertices A, B, C are placed and the horizontal segment AB (blue) is contrasted with the line of sight AC (red). The angle θ = ∠BAC is swept in and labelled to emphasise that the horizontal and the line of sight are two different geometric objects.
media.teaching_notes:
1. WHEN: Play before the student reads the formal definition of line of sight, as an opening hook at the start of Topic T1. It can also be replayed at the beginning of any new heights-and-distances problem to remind students why the diagram must show all three segments.
2. WHAT TO PAUSE: Pause at the 40-second mark, just after the dotted line of sight has been drawn on the minaret scene and before the coordinate grid appears, and ask students to identify which part of the screen shows the horizontal and which shows the line of sight before the labels appear.
3. WHAT TO ASK: "Looking at the scene, can you tell me: is the line of sight the same as the horizontal line at eye level? What is the geometric relationship between them?"

media.instructions_for_student: Watch the video carefully. Pause when the banner appears and try to answer the prediction question before resuming.

media.title: Angle of Elevation: From Looking Straight Ahead to Looking Upward
media.description: An animated concept explainer that begins with a person looking straight ahead at a building wall (θ = 0°, no elevation) and then animates the upward rotation of the line of sight to produce the angle of elevation. The four required diagram elements - observer eye, horizontal, line of sight, and angle of elevation - are highlighted one by one with text callouts so students can identify and name each element in a fresh diagram.
media.teaching_notes:
1. WHEN: Play after the student has completed Topic T1 (line of sight) and before they attempt to draw their first angle-of-elevation diagram independently. Also useful as a quick refresher at the start of any problem-solving session.
2. WHAT TO PAUSE: Pause at the 120-second mark, after the right triangle ABC has appeared and before the four-element spotlight sequence begins, and ask students to name the four geometric elements they see in the diagram.
3. WHAT TO ASK: "Before we label each element together, can you identify which line is the horizontal and which is the line of sight? What is the angle between them called?"

topics.summary: The line of sight; The angle of elevation

content.text:
Let us consider the picture of the minar from the previous chapter, which is redrawn below.

In this figure, the line AC drawn from the eye of the student to the top of the minar is called the line of sight. The student is looking at the top of the minar. The angle BAC, so formed by the line of sight with the horizontal, is called the angle of elevation of the top of the minar from the eye of the student.

Thus, the line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object viewed by the observer.

media.title: Which Ratio to Use: Priya's Mobile Tower - Step-by-Step Decision
media.description: A concept animation walking through Priya the telecom surveyor's scenario to demonstrate the three-branch decision tree for selecting tan, sin, or cos. The animation colour-codes the adjacent side (blue) and the opposite side (red) in each of three scenarios, names the ratio that connects the highlighted pair, and confirms the selection for Priya's specific problem where tan 60° = h/50 gives h = 50√3 m.
media.teaching_notes:
1. WHEN: Play after the student has studied the definitions of sin, cos, and tan from the previous chapter and after completing T1 and T2 in this chapter. Play again during review before any worked example requiring ratio selection.
2. WHAT TO PAUSE: Pause at the 100-second mark, just after all three branches of the decision tree have appeared but before returning to Priya's triangle, and ask students to predict which branch Priya's problem belongs to.
3. WHAT TO ASK: "Why do we choose tan and not sin here? What would happen if we chose sin instead - which side would we need to know that we don't currently have?"

topics.summary: What we need to know, and which ratio to use

content.text:
Let us refer to the picture of the minar again. If you want to find the height CD of the minar without actually measuring it, what information do you need? You would need to know the following:
(i) the distance DE at which the student is standing from the foot of the minar
(ii) the angle of elevation, ∠BAC, of the top of the minar
(iii) the height AE of the student.

Assuming that the above three conditions are known, how can we determine the height of the minar?

In the figure, CD = CB + BD. Here, BD = AE, which is the height of the student.

To find BC, we will use trigonometric ratios of ∠BAC or ∠A.

In △ABC, the side BC is the opposite side in relation to the known ∠A. Now, which of the trigonometric ratios can we use? Which one of them has the two values that we have and the one we need to determine? Our search narrows down to using either tan A or cot A, as these ratios involve AB and BC.

Therefore, tan A = BC/AB or cot A = AB/BC, which on solving would give us BC.

By adding AE to BC, you will get the height of the minar.

Now let us explain the process, we have just discussed, by solving some problems.

media.title: Worked: Finding Tower Height with tan 60° - Animated Solution
media.description: A step-by-step walkthrough of Example 1 (tower problem: BC = 15 m, θ = 60°, find AB). The video follows all five solution steps with a deliberate pause after the labelled diagram is complete so students can predict the ratio selection before it is revealed. The answer AB = 15√3 m is derived and verified with a decimal approximation and a geometric sense-check.
media.teaching_notes:
1. WHEN: Play before the student attempts any similar single-angle tower problems from Exercise 9.1. Play again during review when a student is struggling to select the correct ratio.
2. WHAT TO PAUSE: Pause at the 35-second mark, after the right triangle is fully labelled with BC = 15 m and ∠ACB = 60° but before the ratio selection step appears, and ask students to predict which trigonometric ratio connects the opposite side AB and the adjacent side BC.
3. WHAT TO ASK: "We know BC (adjacent) and want AB (opposite). Which ratio uses exactly these two sides - opposite and adjacent - without involving the hypotenuse?"

content.text: A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground, which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is found to be 60°. Find the height of the tower.
content.question: A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground, which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is found to be 60°. Find the height of the tower.
content.publication_text: A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground, which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is found to be 60°. Find the height of the tower.

content.text:
First let us draw a simple diagram to represent the problem. Here AB represents the tower, CB is the distance of the point from the tower and ∠ACB is the angle of elevation. We need to determine the height of the tower, i.e., AB. Also, ACB is a triangle, right-angled at B.

To solve the problem, we choose the trigonometric ratio tan 60° (or cot 60°), as the ratio involves AB and BC.

Now, tan 60° = AB/BC
i.e., √3 = AB/15
i.e., AB = 15√3
Hence, the height of the tower is 15√3 m.

content.text: An electrician has to repair an electric fault on a pole of height 5 m. She needs to reach a point 1.3 m below the top of the pole to undertake the repair work. What should be the length of the ladder that she should use which, when inclined at an angle of 60° to the horizontal, would enable her to reach the required position? Also, how far from the foot of the pole should she place the foot of the ladder? (You may take √3 = 1.73)

What should be the length of the ladder that she should use which, when inclined at an angle of 60° to the horizontal, would enable her to reach the required position? Also, how far from the foot of the pole should she place the foot of the ladder? (You may take √3 = 1.73)
content.publication_text: An electrician has to repair an electric fault on a pole of height 5 m. She needs to reach a point 1.3 m below the top of the pole to undertake the repair work. What should be the length of the ladder that she should use which, when inclined at an angle of 60° to the horizontal, would enable her to reach the required position? Also, how far from the foot of the pole should she place the foot of the ladder? (You may take √3 = 1.73)

content.text:
In the figure, the electrician is required to reach the point B on the pole AD.
So, BD = AD - AB = (5 - 1.3) m = 3.7 m.
Here, BC represents the ladder. We need to find its length, i.e., the hypotenuse of the right triangle BDC.
Now, can you think which trigonometric ratio should we consider?
It should be sin 60°.
So, BD/BC = sin 60° or 3.7/BC = √3/2
Therefore, BC = (3.7 × 2)/√3 = 4.28 m (approx.)
i.e., the length of the ladder should be 4.28 m.
Now, DC/BD = cot 60° = 1/√3
i.e., DC = 3.7/√3 = 2.14 m (approx.)
Therefore, she should place the foot of the ladder at a distance of 2.14 m from the pole.

content.text: An observer 1.5 m tall is 28.5 m away from a chimney. The angle of elevation of the top of the chimney from her eyes is 45°. What is the height of the chimney?
content.question: An observer 1.5 m tall is 28.5 m away from a chimney. The angle of elevation of the top of the chimney from her eyes is 45°. What is the height of the chimney?
content.publication_text: An observer 1.5 m tall is 28.5 m away from a chimney. The angle of elevation of the top of the chimney from her eyes is 45°. What is the height of the chimney?

content.text:
Here, AB is the chimney, CD the observer and ∠ADE the angle of elevation. In this case, ADE is a triangle, right-angled at E and we are required to find the height of the chimney.
We have AB = AE + BE = AE + 1.5
and DE = CB = 28.5 m
To determine AE, we choose a trigonometric ratio, which involves both AE and DE. Let us choose the tangent of the angle of elevation.
Now, tan 45° = AE/DE
i.e., 1 = AE/28.5
Therefore, AE = 28.5
So the height of the chimney (AB) = (28.5 + 1.5) m = 30 m.

media.title: Angle of Depression: Juhu Beach Lifeguard and Alternate Interior Angles
media.description: An animation introducing the angle of depression through the Juhu Beach lifeguard scenario, then demonstrating the alternate interior angles theorem that equates the angle of depression from the top with the angle of elevation from the base. Parallel horizontal lines are drawn at the observer's level and the ground level, and the line of sight is shown as the transversal, making the alternate angle relationship geometrically obvious.
media.teaching_notes:
1. WHEN: Play before the student encounters any worked example involving angles of depression. Play again whenever a student confuses the angle of depression with the complement of the angle of elevation.
2. WHAT TO PAUSE: Pause at the 110-second mark, after the parallel dashed lines and the transversal have been drawn but before the alternate interior angles are labelled, and ask students to predict which angle at the base equals the angle of depression at the top.
3. WHAT TO ASK: "The two horizontal lines are parallel and the line of sight is the transversal. Using what you know about parallel lines, which pair of angles should be equal here - and what is the name of that angle relationship?"

content.text:
Now, consider the situation from the previous chapter. The girl sitting on the balcony is looking down at a flower pot placed on a stair of the temple. In this case, the line of sight is below the horizontal level. The angle so formed by the line of sight with the horizontal is called the angle of depression.

Thus, the angle of depression of a point on the object being viewed is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the point is below the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we lower our head to look at the point being viewed.

Now, you may identify the lines of sight, and the angles so formed in the third picture from the previous chapter. Are they angles of elevation or angles of depression?

content.text: The angles of depression of the top and the bottom of an 8 m tall building from the top of a multi-storeyed building are 30° and 45°, respectively. Find the height of the multi-storeyed building and the distance between the two buildings.
content.question: The angles of depression of the top and the bottom of an 8 m tall building from the top of a multi-storeyed building are 30° and 45°, respectively. Find the height of the multi-storeyed building and the distance between the two buildings.
content.publication_text: The angles of depression of the top and the bottom of an 8 m tall building from the top of a multi-storeyed building are 30° and 45°, respectively. Find the height of the multi-storeyed building and the distance between the two buildings.

content.text:
In the figure, PC denotes the multi-storyed building and AB denotes the 8 m tall building. We are interested to determine the height of the multi-storeyed building, i.e., PC and the distance between the two buildings, i.e., AC.
Look at the figure carefully. Observe that PB is a transversal to the parallel lines PQ and BD. Therefore, ∠QPB and ∠PBD are alternate angles, and so are equal.
So ∠PBD = 30°. Similarly, ∠PAC = 45°.
In right △PBD, we have
PD/BD = tan 30° = 1/√3 or BD = PD√3
In right △PAC, we have
PC/AC = tan 45° = 1
i.e., PC = AC
Also, PC = PD + DC, therefore, PD + DC = AC.
Since, AC = BD and DC = AB = 8 m, we get PD + 8 = BD = PD√3 (Why?)
This gives PD = 8/(√3 - 1) = 8(√3 + 1)/((√3 + 1)(√3 - 1)) = 4(√3 + 1) m.
So, the height of the multi-storeyed building is {4(√3 + 1) + 8} m = 4(3 + √3) m
and the distance between the two buildings is also 4(3 + √3) m.

This gives PD = 8/(√3 - 1) = 8(√3 + 1)/((√3 + 1)(√3 - 1)) = 4(√3 + 1) m.
So, the height of the multi-storeyed building is {4(√3 + 1) + 8} m = 4(3 + √3) m
and the distance between the two buildings is also 4(3 + √3) m.

content.text: From a point on a bridge across a river, the angles of depression of the banks on opposite sides of the river are 30° and 45°, respectively. If the bridge is at a height of 3 m from the banks, find the width of the river.

content.publication_text: From a point on a bridge across a river, the angles of depression of the banks on opposite sides of the river are 30° and 45°, respectively. If the bridge is at a height of 3 m from the banks, find the width of the river.

content.text:
In the figure, A and B represent points on the bank on opposite sides of the river, so that AB is the width of the river. P is a point on the bridge at a height of 3 m, i.e., DP = 3 m. We are interested to determine the width of the river, which is the length of the side AB of the △APB.
Now, AB = AD + DB
In right △APD, ∠A = 30°.
So, tan 30° = PD/AD
i.e., 1/√3 = 3/AD or AD = 3√3 m
Also, in right △PBD, ∠B = 45°. So, BD = PD = 3 m.
Now, AB = BD + AD = 3 + 3√3 = 3(1 + √3) m.
Therefore, the width of the river is 3(√3 + 1) m.

media.description: A step-by-step walkthrough of Example 4 (flagstaff problem: building AB = 10 m, elevation to AB = 30°, elevation to top of flagstaff BD = 45°, find DB and AP). The video pauses after the first triangle PAB yields AP = 10√3 m so students can predict how AP will be used in the second triangle before the substitution is made. The answer DB = 10(√3 − 1) ≈ 7.32 m is derived and verified.

1. WHEN: Play before the student attempts Q8 (statue and pedestal) or any composite two-elevation-angle problem. The shared-base strategy shown here is the same strategy needed for Q7, Q8, Q9, Q11.

content.text: From a point P on the ground the angle of elevation of the top of a 10 m tall building is 30°. A flag is hoisted at the top of the building and the angle of elevation of the top of the flagstaff from P is 45°. Find the length of the flagstaff and the distance of the building from the point P. (You may take √3 = 1.732)

A flag is hoisted at the top of the building and the angle of elevation of the top of the flagstaff from P is 45°. Find the length of the flagstaff and the distance of the building from the point P. (You may take √3 = 1.732)
content.publication_text: From a point P on the ground the angle of elevation of the top of a 10 m tall building is 30°. A flag is hoisted at the top of the building and the angle of elevation of the top of the flagstaff from P is 45°. Find the length of the flagstaff and the distance of the building from the point P. (You may take √3 = 1.732)

content.text:
In the figure, AB denotes the height of the building, BD the flagstaff and P the given point. Note that there are two right triangles PAB and PAD. We are required to find the length of the flagstaff, i.e., DB and the distance of the building from the point P, i.e., PA.
Since, we know the height of the building AB, we will first consider the right △PAB.
We have tan 30° = AB/AP
i.e., 1/√3 = 10/AP
Therefore, AP = 10√3
i.e., the distance of the building from P is 10√3 m = 17.32 m.
Next, let us suppose DB = x m. Then AD = (10 + x) m.
Now, in right △PAD, tan 45° = AD/AP = (10 + x)/(10√3)
Therefore, 1 = (10 + x)/(10√3)
i.e., x = 10(√3 - 1) = 7.32
So, the length of the flagstaff is 7.32 m.

content.text: The shadow of a tower standing on a level ground is found to be 40 m longer when the Sun's altitude is 30° than when it is 60°. Find the height of the tower.
content.question: The shadow of a tower standing on a level ground is found to be 40 m longer when the Sun's altitude is 30° than when it is 60°. Find the height of the tower.
content.publication_text: The shadow of a tower standing on a level ground is found to be 40 m longer when the Sun's altitude is 30° than when it is 60°. Find the height of the tower.

content.text:
In the figure, AB is the tower and BC is the length of the shadow when the Sun's altitude is 60°, i.e., the angle of elevation of the top of the tower from the tip of the shadow is 60° and DB is the length of the shadow, when the angle of elevation is 30°.
Now, let AB be h m and BC be x m. According to the question, DB is 40 m longer than BC.
So, DB = (40 + x) m
Now, we have two right triangles ABC and ABD.
In △ABC, tan 60° = AB/BC
or, √3 = h/x    (1)
In △ABD, tan 30° = AB/BD
i.e., 1/√3 = h/(x + 40)    (2)
From (1), we have h = x√3
Putting this value in (2), we get (x√3)√3 = x + 40, i.e., 3x = x + 40
i.e., x = 20
So, h = 20√3    [From (1)]
Therefore, the height of the tower is 20√3 m.

content.text:
In this chapter, you have studied the following points:
1. (i) The line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object viewed by the observer.
(ii) The angle of elevation of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when it is above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise our head to look at the object.
(iii) The angle of depression of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when it is below the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we lower our head to look at the object.
2. The height or length of an object or the distance between two distant objects can be determined with the help of trigonometric ratios.
points: (i) The line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object viewed by the observer.
The height or length of an object or the distance between two distant objects can be determined with the help of trigonometric ratios.

object.title: Shadow & Sun Altitude Simulator
object.description: A two-shadow solver. As the sun's altitude changes from 60° to 30°, an object's shadow lengthens; the student sets up a tan equation for each altitude, substitutes h = x√3 from the first into the second, and solves for the height and shadow.
object.teaching_notes: Use after single-triangle problems. At the predict step, ask whether a lower sun gives a longer or shorter shadow. Follow up: the shadow lengthens as the sun drops from 60° to 30° - find the height.
object.generation_prompt: A practice-mode step-based tool for Grade 10 Maths on shadow problems. Palette: indigo triangle, navy numbers, soft grey background.
object.instructions_for_student: Write a tan equation for each sun altitude, substitute one into the other, and solve for the height and shadow. Predict how the shadow changes first.

object.title: Two-Triangle Problem Solver
object.description: A composite-figure solver. A problem with two right triangles sharing a side (for example two angles of elevation to the top and bottom of a flagstaff) is set up; the student writes a tan equation for each triangle and combines them to find the unknown height or distance.
object.teaching_notes: Use for Exercise 9.1 Q7-Q11. At the predict step, check students share the common side between the two equations. Follow up: find the flagstaff height from two elevation angles.
object.generation_prompt: A practice-mode step-based tool for Grade 10 Maths on two-triangle problems. UI: a labelled figure with two right triangles, a tan equation per triangle, and a combine-and-solve step; a predict step asks which quantity to eliminate. Palette: indigo triangles, navy numbers, soft grey background.
object.instructions_for_student: Write a tan equation for each right triangle, then combine them to eliminate the common side and solve. Predict what cancels first.

object.title: Moving Object Tracker (time-based problems)
object.description: A moving-object solver. As a car approaches a tower, two angles of elevation are measured a time apart; the student writes both horizontal distances in terms of the tower height h, forms their ratio so h cancels, and finds the remaining time or distance.

examples: car approaching a tower, two elevation angles

object.teaching_notes: Use for moving-object problems. At the predict step, check students express both distances in terms of h. Follow up: find the time for the car to reach the tower.
object.generation_prompt: A practice-mode step-based tool for Grade 10 Maths on time-based trig problems. UI: a scene with a tower and a moving car at two positions, tan equations giving distances in terms of h, and a ratio step where h cancels; a predict step asks what cancels. Palette: indigo triangle, navy numbers, soft grey background.
object.instructions_for_student: Express both horizontal distances in terms of the tower height h, form their ratio so h cancels, and solve for the time or distance. Predict what cancels first.

carried_over_topics.topic_name: Line of Sight: Definition and Geometric Representation
carried_over_topics.brief_summary: In this topic, students define the line of sight as the straight segment from the observer's eye to the viewed point and distinguish it from the horizontal at eye level.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK

Consider a visitor standing on the paved path near Qutub Minar in Delhi, approximately 72 metres from its base. The visitor raises their eyes upward to look at the very tip of the minaret rising far above. A clear, straight imaginary line can be drawn from the visitor's eyes all the way to the top of the minaret. This line is not horizontal - it slants upward at an angle. This single geometric segment, stretching directly from the observer's eye to the point being viewed, is the starting point for every heights-and-distances problem in this chapter.

RECALL

In the previous chapter, you studied trigonometric ratios: sine, cosine, tangent, and their reciprocals, defined with respect to an angle in a right-angled triangle. In this chapter, you will apply those ratios to solve practical problems involving the heights of structures and the distances between objects that cannot be measured directly. The key to setting up each such problem correctly is understanding two foundational ideas: the line of sight and the angle of elevation.

CORE

The line of sight is the straight line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object being viewed by the observer.

To understand this definition precisely, consider Fig. 9.1 from the textbook. In that figure, the line AC is drawn from the eye of a student (positioned at point A) to the top of a minar (located at point C). This line AC is the line of sight. It is a directed geometric segment - it begins at the observer's eye and ends at the object being observed. It does not follow the ground; it does not follow any wall or surface. It is simply the most direct imaginary path between the observer's eye and the point being viewed, travelling through the air in a straight line.

The following distinctions are important and must be kept in mind throughout this chapter:

(i) The line of sight always starts at the observer's eye, not at the observer's feet or any other reference point.

(ii) The line of sight is drawn to a specific point on the object - typically its top, its base, or another clearly defined point.

(iii) The line of sight is distinct from the horizontal. In the Qutub Minar example, the horizontal would be a perfectly flat line extending in front of the observer at eye level. The line of sight, however, is tilted upward because the top of the minaret is above the observer's horizontal level.

Convention for this chapter: Let h denote an unknown vertical height, d denote a known horizontal distance, and θ denote the given angle of elevation.

ERROR ALERT

A common error is to confuse the line of sight with the horizontal line at eye level. These are two different lines. The horizontal is always perfectly flat, extending at the observer's eye level in the direction of the object. The line of sight is an oblique line that rises above the horizontal (when the observer looks upward) or drops below the horizontal (when the observer looks downward). In all problems involving angle of elevation - which is the focus of Module 1 - the line of sight rises above the horizontal. Do not draw the line of sight along the ground or along the horizontal; always draw it as a slanted line from the observer's eye to the point being viewed.

CHECK

To consolidate your understanding, answer the following: In Fig. 9.1, the student stands at point A and looks at the top of the minar at point C. Name the line of sight. Now identify the horizontal line. Are they the same line? If not, what is the geometric relationship between them? (They originate from the same point A but travel in different directions, forming an angle between them - and that angle is the angle of elevation, which you will define next.)
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
9.1 Heights and Distances

In the previous chapter, you have studied about trigonometric ratios. In this chapter, you will be studying about some ways in which trigonometry is used in the life around you.

Let us consider Fig. 8.1 of prvious chapter, which is redrawn below in Fig. 9.1.

In this figure, the line AC drawn from the eye of the student to the top of the minar is called the line of sight. The student is looking at the top of the minar. The angle BAC, so formed by the line of sight with the horizontal, is called the angle of elevation of the top of the minar from the eye of the student.

Thus, the line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object viewed by the observer.
concept_bullets: The line of sight is the straight segment from the observer's eye to the viewed point. For observer at A and minar top at C, line AC is the line of sight, not the ground segment from A to the minar base.
The line of sight is distinct from the horizontal at eye level. Both start at A but the horizontal AB is flat while the line of sight AC slants upward, forming angle ∠BAC = θ between them.
The line of sight always begins at the observer's eye, not feet. If the observer stands 1.5 m tall, the line of sight starts 1.5 m above the ground, not at ground level.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: The line of sight is introduced as the foundational concept of the chapter: a directed segment beginning at the observer's eye and ending at the point being observed, passing through the air in a straight line. Using the Qutub Minar scenario with observer at A and minar top at C, students see that the line AC is the line of sight, while AB is the horizontal at eye level, and these two lines are distinct - they originate from A but travel in different directions, forming an angle at A. Three distinctions are critical: the line of sight starts at the observer's eye (not the feet), it is drawn to a specific point on the object, and it is oblique (not flat). Students must avoid the most common error of confusing the line of sight with the horizontal, which are two different geometric segments that meet at the observer's eye.
important_points: the line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object viewed by the observer
In this figure, the line AC drawn from the eye of the student to the top of the minar is called the line of sight.
The angle BAC, so formed by the line of sight with the horizontal, is called the angle of elevation of the top of the minar from the eye of the student.

recall_questions.answer: The line of sight is the straight line drawn from the eye of the observer to the specific point in the object being viewed. It is directed from the observer's eye to the viewed point and travels through the air in a straight line. The horizontal at eye level is a perfectly flat line extending from the observer's eye in the direction of the object at the same height as the observer's eye. The key difference is direction: the horizontal is always flat (0° inclination), while the line of sight is oblique - it tilts upward when the observer looks at a point above eye level, or downward when looking at a point below eye level. They originate from the same point (the observer's eye) but travel in different directions, forming an angle between them.

recall_questions.answer: The diagram is a right triangle with: vertex A at the observer's position on the left, vertex B directly below C on the right (right angle at B), and vertex C at the top of the minaret. Segment AC is the line of sight (from observer's eye to the top of the minaret - oblique, slanting upward). Segment AB is the horizontal at eye level (flat, from A to B). Segment BC is the vertical height of the minaret above eye level. The angle at vertex A between AB (horizontal) and AC (line of sight) is the angle formed between the line of sight and the horizontal. carried_over_topics.topic_name: Angle of Elevation: Definition, Diagram, and Setup
carried_over_topics.brief_summary: In this topic, students define the angle of elevation as the upward angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when the viewed object is above the observer.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK

Imagine standing at the base of a tall building and tilting your head upward to look at the rooftop. Your eyes, following the line of sight, naturally rise above the flat horizontal level in front of you. The angle through which your line of sight has turned upward from the horizontal captures exactly how steeply you are looking. This angle has a precise name and a precise definition in mathematics.

RECALL

From T1, you know that the line of sight is the straight line from the observer's eye to the point being viewed. You also know that the horizontal is a flat line at eye level. Whenever the point being viewed lies above the observer's horizontal level - as is the case when looking at a tall tower, a minaret, or a mountain peak - the line of sight tilts upward relative to the horizontal, and the angle between them is meaningful and measurable.

CORE

The angle of elevation of a point being viewed is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the point being viewed is above the horizontal level of the observer - that is, when the observer raises their head to look at the object (see Fig. 9.2).

To visualise this precisely, refer to Fig. 9.1. In that figure, the line AC is the line of sight from the student's eye at A to the top of the minar at C. The line AB is the horizontal at the student's eye level. The angle BAC - measured between the horizontal AB and the line of sight AC - is the angle of elevation of the top of the minar from the student's eye.

Four elements must be correctly identified and labelled in any diagram for an angle-of-elevation problem:

(i) The observer's eye position - the point from which the line of sight originates (e.g., point A).
(ii) The horizontal line at eye level - a flat line drawn from the observer's eye in the direction of the object (e.g., line AB).
(iii) The line of sight - the slanted line from the observer's eye to the top of the object (e.g., line AC).
(iv) The angle of elevation - the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight, measured upward from the horizontal (e.g., ∠BAC).

Variable convention: In all diagrams and problems in this chapter, h denotes the unknown vertical height, d denotes the known horizontal distance, and θ denotes the given angle of elevation.

Setting up the right triangle: Because the object (e.g., a tower) stands vertically and the ground is horizontal, the vertical height, the horizontal distance, and the line of sight form a right-angled triangle. The right angle is always at the base of the vertical structure. This triangle is the core geometric object used in all height-and-distance calculations.

ERROR ALERT

A common error is to measure the angle of elevation from the line of sight back to the vertical structure, rather than from the horizontal. Always measure the angle of elevation from the horizontal line at eye level upward to the line of sight. The angle is formed at the observer's eye, between the horizontal and the line of sight - not at the base of the object, not at the top of the object.

CHECK

In a diagram based on Fig. 9.1, label the following: the observer's eye at A, the horizontal line at AB, the line of sight AC to the top of the minar at C, and the angle of elevation ∠BAC = θ. Now identify which side of the right triangle is opposite to θ, which side is adjacent to θ, and which side is the hypotenuse. This labelling will be essential when you choose the correct trigonometric ratio in T3.

recall_questions.answer: The angle of elevation of a point being viewed is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the point being viewed is above the horizontal level of the observer - that is, when the observer raises their head to look at the object. It is always measured upward from the horizontal to the line of sight.

recall_questions.answer: In right triangle ABC with the right angle at B and angle θ = 45° at A: The side opposite to θ (at A) is BC (the vertical height of the building, because it is the side across from A and does not touch the angle at A). The side adjacent to θ (at A) is AB (the horizontal distance = 20 m, because it forms one arm of the angle at A and is not the hypotenuse). The hypotenuse is AC (the line of sight, the side opposite the right angle at B). The ratio that connects the opposite side (BC) and the adjacent side (AB) without using the hypotenuse is: tan θ = opposite / adjacent = BC / AB. Therefore, tan 45° = BC / 20, giving BC = 20 × tan 45° = 20 × 1 = 20 m.

carried_over_topics.brief_summary: In this topic, students select the correct trigonometric ratio - tan, sin, or cos - for a heights-and-distances problem by identifying which two sides of the right triangle are known and unknown.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK

Priya is a telecom surveyor working in Pune. She has been assigned to verify the height of a newly erected mobile tower. Standing on flat ground exactly 50 metres from the base of the tower, she uses a clinometer to measure the angle of elevation to the top of the tower as 60°. She knows the horizontal distance (50 m) and the angle of elevation (60°). The height of the tower is unknown. Her task is to choose the correct trigonometric ratio to connect these three quantities and then solve for the unknown height. The decision she must make - which ratio to use - is precisely what this topic addresses.

RECALL

From your previous chapter on trigonometric ratios, you know that for an acute angle θ in a right-angled triangle:

sin θ = opposite side / hypotenuse
cos θ = adjacent side / hypotenuse
tan θ = opposite side / adjacent side

The key words here are "opposite", "adjacent", and "hypotenuse", all defined relative to the angle θ. Before choosing a ratio, you must correctly identify which side is opposite to θ and which side is adjacent to θ in your triangle.

CORE

Consider Fig. 9.1. The student stands at A, the minar stands with its foot at E and its top at C. The segment BD (where D is on the minar and B is at the base-level directly below A) represents the height of the minar above the student's eye level, here called BC in the right triangle ABC. The student is at A, the right angle is at B, and the height BC is the vertical side.

To find the height of the minar without measuring it directly, three pieces of information are needed:
(i) the distance DE at which the student is standing from the foot of the minar
(ii) the angle of elevation, ∠ BAC, of the top of the minar
(iii) the height AE of the student.

Once these are known, the geometry gives: CD = CB + BD, where BD = AE (the student's height).

To find BC, the relevant right triangle is △ ABC, where:
- ∠ BAC = θ is the angle of elevation
- BC is the side opposite to θ (the unknown height above eye level, denoted h)
- AB is the side adjacent to θ (the horizontal distance, denoted d)
- AC is the hypotenuse (the line of sight)

Now, which trigonometric ratio involves the two known or sought quantities? Ask this question systematically:

Step 1 - What do I know? The horizontal distance AB = d.
Step 2 - What do I want to find? The vertical height BC = h.
Step 3 - Which ratio links opposite and adjacent (i.e., h and d)? That is tan θ.

Therefore, tan A = BC/AB, or equivalently cot A = AB/BC.

Using tan A = BC/AB and solving gives BC, the height of the minar above eye level. Adding AE (the student's height) to BC then gives the total height of the minar, CD.

If, instead, the hypotenuse (line-of-sight distance) were the unknown, then sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse would be the appropriate ratio. If the hypotenuse were known and the adjacent side were the unknown, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse would be used. The decision tree is:

- Known: d (adjacent), Unknown: h (opposite) → use tan θ = h/d
- Known: hypotenuse (line-of-sight), Unknown: h (opposite) → use sin θ = h/hypotenuse
- Known: hypotenuse, Unknown: d (adjacent) → use cos θ = d/hypotenuse

In Priya's mobile-tower example, the known side is the horizontal base (50 m, adjacent to θ) and the unknown is the tower height (opposite to θ). There is no information about the hypotenuse. Therefore, tan 60° = h/50, giving h = 50 tan 60° = 50√3 m. This is the correct and efficient choice.

ERROR ALERT

A common error is to confuse which side is "opposite" and which side is "adjacent" relative to the angle θ. Remember: "opposite" means the side directly across from the angle θ (not touching θ), while "adjacent" means the side that forms one arm of the angle θ (the non-hypotenuse arm). If you mislabel these sides, you will select the wrong ratio and obtain an incorrect answer. Always draw and label the triangle first - mark the angle θ, then identify opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse before writing any equation.

CHECK

In △ ABC with right angle at B, ∠BAC = 60°, and AB = 50 m: (a) Which side is opposite to 60°? (b) Which side is adjacent to 60°? (c) Write down the ratio that connects these two sides. (d) If tan 60° = √3, what is the value of BC? Compare your answer with Priya's result of 50√3 m. If they agree, your ratio selection is correct.
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
Now, you may identify the lines of sight, and the angles so formed in Fig. 8.3. Are they angles of elevation or angles of depression?

Let us refer to Fig. 9.1 again. If you want to find the height CD of the minar without actually measuring it, what information do you need? You would need to know the following:
(i) the distance DE at which the student is standing from the foot of the minar
(ii) the angle of elevation, ∠ BAC, of the top of the minar
(iii) the height AE of the student.

Assuming that the above three conditions are known, how can we determine the height of the minar?

In the figure, CD = CB + BD. Here, BD = AE, which is the height of the student.

To find BC, we will use trigonometric ratios of ∠ BAC or ∠ A.

In ∆ ABC, the side BC is the opposite side in relation to the known ∠ A. Now, which of the trigonometric ratios can we use? Which one of them has the two values that we have and the one we need to determine? Our search narrows down to using either tan A or cot A, as these ratios involve AB and BC.

Therefore, tan A = BC/AB or cot A = AB/BC, which on solving would give us BC.

By adding AE to BC, you will get the height of the minar.

Now let us explain the process, we have just discussed, by solving some problems.
concept_bullets: If horizontal distance d is known and height h is unknown, use tan θ = h/d. For d = 50 m, θ = 60°: h = 50 tan 60° = 50√3 m.
If the hypotenuse (line-of-sight or rope length) is known and height h is unknown, use sin θ = h/hypotenuse. For hypotenuse = 20 m, θ = 30°: h = 20 × (1/2) = 10 m.
If the hypotenuse is known and horizontal distance d is unknown, use cos θ = d/hypotenuse. For hypotenuse = 20 m, θ = 30°: d = 20 cos 30° = 10√3 m.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: The ratio-selection decision tree is the procedural core of the chapter: when opposite and adjacent sides are involved (height and horizontal distance), use tan θ = h/d; when the hypotenuse is unknown and the opposite side is known, use sin θ = h/hypotenuse; when the adjacent side is unknown and the hypotenuse is known, use cos θ = d/hypotenuse. Students apply this tree to the minar example, where the student's height offset (AE) must be added back to get the full minar height after computing BC from tan. The three-step process - identify known side, identify unknown side, select the ratio that links those two - is introduced and practised through the mobile tower worked example: tan 60° = h/50 gives h = 50√3 m. A critical error is mislabelling opposite and adjacent relative to θ, which reverses the ratio and produces a wrong answer.
important_points: To find BC, we will use trigonometric ratios of ∠ BAC or ∠ A.
Our search narrows down to using either tan A or cot A, as these ratios involve AB and BC.
Therefore, tan A = BC/AB or cot A = AB/BC, which on solving would give us BC.

recall_questions.answer: The decision rule is: Step 1 - identify which two sides are involved (one known, one unknown). Step 2 - apply the rule: If the known side is the adjacent (horizontal distance) and the unknown is the opposite (height), use tan θ = opposite / adjacent. If the known side is the hypotenuse (line-of-sight length) and the unknown is the opposite (height), use sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse. If the known side is the hypotenuse and the unknown is the adjacent (horizontal distance), use cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle (the line of sight); the opposite and adjacent sides are identified relative to the given angle θ.
recall_questions.prompt: Describe the decision rule for selecting which trigonometric ratio - tan, sin, or cos - to use in a heights-and-distances problem, based on which two sides of the right triangle?

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 - Draw and label: right triangle with observer at A, foot of tower at B (right angle), top at C. θ = ∠BAC = 60°. Known: AB = 50 m (adjacent to θ). Unknown: BC = h (opposite to θ). Step 2 - Justify ratio: The known side is the adjacent side (AB = 50 m) and the unknown side is the opposite side (BC = h). The hypotenuse AC is neither given nor required. Therefore, the correct ratio is tan θ = opposite / adjacent, i.e., tan 60° = BC / AB. Step 3 - Set up equation: tan 60° = h / 50. Step 4 - Substitute tan 60° = √3: √3 = h / 50. Step 5 - Solve: h = 50√3 m. The height of the tower is 50√3 m (approximately 86.6 m). If sin or cos were used instead, the hypotenuse (unknown) would appear in the equation, introducing a second unknown and making the problem unsolvable in one step.
recall_questions.prompt: A surveyor stands 50 m from the base of a mobile tower and measures the angle of elevation as 60°. Justify which trigonometric ratio to use, identify the known and unknown sides relative to the angle, and calculate the height of the tower. Show all working.

recall_questions.answer: Student A is correct. In the right triangle for this problem, the known side is the adjacent side (horizontal distance = 50 m) and the unknown side is the opposite side (tower height = h). tan θ = opposite / adjacent = h / 50 is the correct ratio because it directly connects the two sides in question without involving the hypotenuse. Student B is incorrect. sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse = h / (line-of-sight distance). For sin 60° = h / 50 to be valid, the 50 m must be the hypotenuse (line-of-sight distance), but in this problem 50 m is the horizontal ground distance, which is the adjacent side - not the hypotenuse. Student B has misidentified which side is 50 m. The hypotenuse (line of sight) is longer than the horizontal distance and is not given in this problem. Therefore, Student A's setup tan 60° = h/50 → h = 50√3 m is correct, and Student B's setup gives the wrong answer.
recall_questions.prompt: Two students solve the same tower problem (horizontal distance 50 m, angle of elevation 60°). Student A writes tan 60° = h/50. Student B writes sin 60° = h/50. Explain which student is correct and why the other student's ratio selection leads to a wrong answer.

carried_over_topics.brief_summary: Students work through a tower height problem where tan 60° and a 15 m horizontal distance give a tower height of 15√3 m using a five-step right-triangle procedure.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
WORKED EXAMPLE 1

Example 1: A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground, which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is found to be 60°. Find the height of the tower.

STEP 1: Draw a right triangle and label all quantities.

Draw a simple diagram as shown in Fig. 9.4. In this diagram, AB represents the tower standing vertically on the ground. Point C is the observation point on the ground, at a horizontal distance of 15 m from the foot of the tower B. The line of sight goes from C to A (the top of the tower). The angle ∠ACB = 60° is the angle of elevation. Triangle ACB is right-angled at B.

Label the known and unknown quantities using the established variable conventions:
- h = AB = height of the tower (unknown)
- d = BC = 15 m (horizontal distance, known)
- θ = ∠ACB = 60° (angle of elevation, known)

WHY THIS STEP? Drawing a labelled diagram before writing any equation is not optional - it is the most important step. A correct diagram prevents you from assigning quantities to the wrong sides of the triangle, which is the most common source of error in heights-and-distances problems. Take your time setting up the diagram.

STEP 2: Identify the known and unknown quantities from the diagram.

Known: d = BC = 15 m and θ = 60°.
Unknown: h = AB.

WHY THIS STEP? Explicitly listing known and unknown quantities forces you to check whether you have sufficient information to solve the problem before committing to a ratio.

STEP 3: Choose the appropriate trigonometric ratio.

In △ ACB (right-angled at B), with respect to angle θ = ∠ACB:
- The side opposite to θ is AB = h (unknown).
- The side adjacent to θ is BC = d = 15 m (known).
- The hypotenuse is AC (the line of sight, not needed here).

Since the known side is the adjacent side and the unknown side is the opposite side, the ratio that links them is:

tan θ = opposite / adjacent = AB / BC

WHY THIS STEP? You choose tan because it is the only standard ratio that directly connects the opposite side and the adjacent side, without involving the hypotenuse. Using sin or cos here would introduce a third unknown (the hypotenuse) and complicate the equation unnecessarily.

STEP 4: Set up the equation.

tan 60° = AB/BC

i.e., √3 = AB/15

WHY THIS STEP? The equation is formed by substituting the known value of tan 60° and the known horizontal distance directly into the ratio formula. No other substitution is needed at this stage.

STEP 5: Solve for the unknown.

i.e., AB = 15√3

Hence, the height of the tower is 15√3 m.

CHECK: Does the answer make physical sense? A horizontal distance of 15 m and an angle of elevation of 60° mean the tower is quite steep relative to the observer. tan 60° = √3 ≈ 1.732, so h = 15 × 1.732 ≈ 25.98 m. A tower roughly 26 m tall visible at an angle of 60° from 15 m away is geometrically consistent - the height is approximately 1.73 times the horizontal distance, which matches the steepness implied by a 60° angle. The answer is physically reasonable.

ERROR ALERT

A common error in problems like this is to write tan 60° = BC/AB (i.e., to write the adjacent side over the opposite side) instead of tan 60° = AB/BC. Always recall: tan θ = opposite/adjacent. The opposite side to the angle at C is the vertical height AB, not the horizontal distance BC. If you invert the ratio, you will obtain h = 15/√3 = 5√3 m ≈ 8.66 m, which significantly underestimates the true height.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 (PARTIALLY FADED)

Problem: A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground 30 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is 30°. Find the height of the tower.

STEP 1: Draw a right triangle. Label h = height of tower (unknown), d = 30 m (horizontal distance), θ = 30°.

STEP 2: Known: d = 30 m, θ = 30°. Unknown: h.

STEP 3: [Student to complete] Which trigonometric ratio connects the opposite side (h) and the adjacent side (d)? Write the ratio name and its formula.

STEP 4: Set up the equation.
tan 30° = h/30
i.e., 1/√3 = h/30

STEP 5: [Student to complete] Solve for h. Express the answer in simplified form.

(Answer: h = 30/√3 = 10√3 m)

recall_questions.prompt: A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top is 60°. Calculate the height of the tower. Show all five steps of the solution.

recall_questions.answer: The student inverted the tangent ratio. The correct formula is tan θ = opposite / adjacent. In the right triangle, the angle of elevation θ = 60° is at C (the observer). The side opposite to the angle at C is AB (the tower height = h), and the side adjacent to the angle at C is BC (= 15 m). Therefore, tan 60° = AB / BC = h / 15, not BC / AB = 15 / h. The student wrote the ratio upside down (adjacent over opposite instead of opposite over adjacent). The correct equation is: √3 = h / 15, giving h = 15√3 m ≈ 25.98 m. The student's answer of 5√3 ≈ 8.66 m significantly underestimates the true height.

carried_over_topics.brief_summary: Students work through an electrician pole problem finding ladder length using sin 60° and base distance using cot 60°, with a Pythagoras verification of both results.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
WORKED EXAMPLE 1

Example 2: An electrician has to repair an electric fault on a pole of height 5 m. She needs to reach a point 1.3 m below the top of the pole to undertake the repair work (see Fig. 9.5). What should be the length of the ladder that she should use which, when inclined at an angle of 60° to the horizontal, would enable her to reach the required position? Also, how far from the foot of the pole should she place the foot of the ladder? (You may take √3 = 1.73)

STEP 1: Draw a right triangle and label all quantities.

In Fig. 9.5, the pole is represented by AD, with A at the top and D at the foot. The electrician needs to reach point B on the pole, where B is 1.3 m below the top A. Therefore:

BD = AD − AB = (5 − 1.3) m = 3.7 m

The ladder is represented by BC, inclined at 60° to the horizontal, with its top at B and its foot at C on the ground. Triangle BDC is right-angled at D.

Label quantities:
- h = BD = 3.7 m (known vertical height from ground to repair point)
- d = DC = horizontal distance from foot of pole to foot of ladder (unknown)
- Ladder length = BC = hypotenuse (unknown)
- θ = ∠BCD = 60° (angle of inclination to the horizontal, i.e., angle of elevation)

WHY THIS STEP? Identifying the correct triangle is critical here. The relevant right triangle is △BDC, not △ADC. The electrician needs to reach B, not A. Always re-read the problem to locate the correct target point before drawing.

STEP 2: Identify the known and unknown quantities.

Known: BD = 3.7 m (opposite side to θ), θ = 60°.
First unknown: BC (hypotenuse = ladder length).
Second unknown: DC (adjacent side = foot-of-ladder distance).

WHY THIS STEP? This problem has two unknowns, requiring two separate equations. Identify both unknowns explicitly before solving.

STEP 3: Choose the appropriate trigonometric ratio for the first unknown (ladder length BC).

Since the known side is BD (opposite to θ) and the unknown is BC (hypotenuse), the ratio linking opposite and hypotenuse is:

sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse = BD / BC

WHY THIS STEP? You choose sin because the known side is the opposite side and the unknown is the hypotenuse. Using tan would introduce DC (another unknown) and not isolate BC directly.

STEP 4: Set up and solve for the ladder length BC.

So, BD/BC = sin 60° or 3.7/BC = √3/2

Therefore, BC = (3.7 × 2)/√3 = 4.28 m (approx.)

i.e., the length of the ladder should be 4.28 m.

WHY THIS STEP? After cross-multiplying 3.7/BC = √3/2, you obtain BC = (3.7 × 2)/√3. Substituting √3 ≈ 1.73 gives BC ≈ 7.4/1.73 ≈ 4.28 m.

STEP 5: Choose the appropriate trigonometric ratio for the second unknown (DC, foot-of-ladder distance).

Now, DC/BD = cot 60° = 1/√3

i.e., DC = 3.7/√3 = 2.14 m (approx.)

Therefore, she should place the foot of the ladder at a distance of 2.14 m from the pole.

CHECK: Does the answer make physical sense? With BD = 3.7 m and θ = 60°, the ladder leans steeply, so the foot should be relatively close to the pole. DC ≈ 2.14 m is less than BD = 3.7 m, which is consistent with a steep 60° inclination. Also, verify using Pythagoras: BC² = BD² + DC² = (3.7)² + (2.14)² = 13.69 + 4.58 = 18.27, and BC ≈ √18.27 ≈ 4.27 m, which matches 4.28 m (difference due to rounding). The answer is physically and mathematically consistent.

ERROR ALERT

A common error in this type of problem is to use tan 60° instead of sin 60° when finding the ladder length. Students sometimes write tan 60° = BD/DC and then try to find BC separately - this is an indirect and more cumbersome route. When the hypotenuse is the unknown, always reach for sin or cos first. Specifically: if you know the opposite side and want the hypotenuse, use sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse. If you know the adjacent side and want the hypotenuse, use cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse. Applying tan in place of sin here would give an incorrect setup.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 (PARTIALLY FADED)

Problem: A ramp is to be built at a construction site. The ramp must rise to a height of 2.4 m above the ground and is to be inclined at 45° to the horizontal. Find the length of the ramp (hypotenuse) and the horizontal distance covered at the base.

STEP 1: Draw a right triangle. Label: vertical height = 2.4 m (opposite), angle of inclination = 45°, ramp length = hypotenuse (unknown), base = adjacent (unknown).

STEP 2: Known: opposite side = 2.4 m, θ = 45°. Unknown: hypotenuse (ramp length), adjacent (base distance).

STEP 3: [Student to complete] Which ratio connects the opposite side (2.4 m) and the hypotenuse? Write the equation.

STEP 4: Solve for the ramp length.
sin 45° = 2.4 / ramp length
1/√2 = 2.4 / ramp length
Ramp length = 2.4√2 ≈ 3.39 m

STEP 5: [Student to complete] Using cot 45° or tan 45°, find the base distance. Show your working.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 - Diagram: Right triangle BDC. B = repair point, D = foot of pole (right angle), C = foot of ladder. Label: BD = 3.7 m (opposite to ∠BCD = 60°), BC = ladder length (hypotenuse, unknown), DC = base distance (adjacent, unknown). Step 2 - Known: BD = 3.7 m (opposite), θ = 60°. First unknown: BC (hypotenuse). Second unknown: DC (adjacent). Step 3 - Ratio for BC: Known side is opposite (BD), unknown is hypotenuse (BC). Use sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse. Step 4 - Solve for BC: sin 60° = BD / BC → 3.7 / BC = √3 / 2 → BC = (3.7 × 2) / √3 = 7.4 / 1.73 ≈ 4.28 m. Step 5 - Ratio for DC: cot 60° = DC / BD → DC = BD / tan 60° = 3.7 / √3 = 3.7 / 1.73 ≈ 2.14 m. The ladder length is approximately 4.28 m and its foot should be placed approximately 2.14 m from the pole.
recall_questions.prompt: An electrician needs to reach a point 3.7 m above the ground on a vertical pole. She places a ladder inclined at 60° to the horizontal. Calculate the length of the ladder and the distance from the foot of the pole to the foot of the ladder. Show all working.

recall_questions.answer: sin 60° is used because the known side is the vertical height BD = 3.7 m (opposite to the 60° angle at C) and the unknown is the ladder length BC (hypotenuse, i.e., the side opposite the right angle at D). sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse directly connects these two sides. If tan 60° were used instead, the equation would be tan 60° = BD / DC = 3.7 / DC, which would find the adjacent side DC (the base distance) - not the ladder length. To then find the ladder length, one would need an additional step using Pythagoras or sin, making the solution indirect and more complex. Additionally, using tan 60° = BC / BD (confusing which side is the hypotenuse) would produce an entirely wrong equation. The direct and efficient choice when the known side is the opposite and the unknown is the hypotenuse is always sin θ.

carried_over_topics.brief_summary: Students work through an observer-offset chimney problem where the observer's height of 1.5 m is added to the computed height AE = 28.5 m giving total chimney height 30 m.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
WORKED EXAMPLE 1

Example 3: An observer 1.5 m tall is 28.5 m away from a chimney. The angle of elevation of the top of the chimney from her eyes is 45°. What is the height of the chimney?

STEP 1: Draw a right triangle and label all quantities.

In Fig. 9.6, AB represents the chimney, and CD represents the observer of height 1.5 m standing at a horizontal distance of 28.5 m from the base of the chimney. The observer's eyes are at point D. The horizontal line at eye level is DE. The angle of elevation ∠ADE = 45° is measured from DE (horizontal at eye level) to DA (the line of sight to the top of the chimney at A).

Because D is at eye level (1.5 m above the ground) and E is the point on the chimney at the same height as D, the right-angled triangle for this problem is △ADE, right-angled at E.

Label quantities:
- AE = vertical height of chimney above eye level (unknown) - denote as h₁
- DE = CB = 28.5 m (horizontal distance at eye level, known) - denote as d
- θ = ∠ADE = 45° (angle of elevation from observer's eyes, known)
- BE = CD = 1.5 m (observer's height, known)
- Total chimney height AB = AE + BE = AE + 1.5 m

Convention applied: h denotes the portion of the chimney height above the observer's eye level (i.e., AE = h₁), and the total height of the chimney is h₁ + 1.5 m.

WHY THIS STEP? This problem has an important structural feature: the observer is not at ground level. Their eyes are 1.5 m above the ground. This means the right triangle is formed between the observer's eye level (D) and the top of the chimney (A), not between the ground and the top of the chimney. The height of the chimney must be decomposed into two parts: the height of the chimney above eye level (AE) and the observer's own height (BE = CD). Never forget to add the observer's height back at the end.

We have AB = AE + BE = AE + 1.5
and DE = CB = 28.5 m

STEP 2: Identify the known and unknown quantities.

Known: d = DE = 28.5 m (adjacent to θ), θ = 45°.
Unknown: h₁ = AE (opposite to θ).
Final answer required: AB = h₁ + 1.5.

WHY THIS STEP? Listing all quantities at this stage, including the two-part decomposition of the total height, prevents the error of forgetting to add the observer's eye-level height at the end.

STEP 3: Choose the appropriate trigonometric ratio.

In △ ADE (right-angled at E), the known side is DE (adjacent to θ) and the unknown side is AE (opposite to θ). The ratio linking opposite and adjacent is:

tan θ = opposite / adjacent = AE / DE

WHY THIS STEP? Since both the known side (adjacent) and the unknown side (opposite) are present, and the hypotenuse is not needed, tan is the efficient and direct choice.

STEP 4: Set up the equation.

To determine AE, we choose a trigonometric ratio, which involves both AE and DE. Let us choose the tangent of the angle of elevation.

Now, tan 45° = AE/DE

i.e., 1 = AE/28.5

WHY THIS STEP? tan 45° = 1 is a standard value from the trigonometric table studied in the previous chapter. Substituting it directly gives a one-step equation.

STEP 5: Solve for the unknown and find the total chimney height.

Therefore, AE = 28.5

So the height of the chimney (AB) = (28.5 + 1.5) m = 30 m.

CHECK: Does the answer make physical sense? The angle of elevation is 45°, which means the chimney height above eye level should equal the horizontal distance to the chimney (since tan 45° = 1). The horizontal distance is 28.5 m, and AE = 28.5 m - these are equal, which is exactly what tan 45° = 1 requires. Adding 1.5 m for the observer's height gives 30 m total. The answer is geometrically correct and physically sensible.

ERROR ALERT

The most common error in observer-offset problems is to forget to add the observer's height (CD = 1.5 m) to the computed height AE. Students correctly find AE = 28.5 m and then report it as the final answer - arriving at 28.5 m instead of the correct 30 m. Always re-read the question: it asks for the total height of the chimney (AB), which equals the height above the observer's eye level (AE) plus the observer's own height (BE = CD = 1.5 m). A second related error is to compute the angle of elevation from the ground level rather than from the observer's eye level. The angle of elevation is always measured from the observer's horizontal at eye level, not from the ground.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 (PARTIALLY FADED)

Problem: A boy 1.2 m tall stands 24 m from the foot of a tower. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from the boy's eyes is 30°. Find the total height of the tower.

STEP 1: Draw a right triangle. Label: observer's eye height = 1.2 m above ground, horizontal distance = 24 m, angle of elevation = 30°, height above eye level = h₁ (unknown), total tower height = h₁ + 1.2 m.

STEP 2: Known: d = 24 m (adjacent), θ = 30°. Unknown: h₁ = height above eye level.

STEP 3: [Student to complete] Write the trigonometric equation that links h₁ and d using tan 30°.

STEP 4: tan 30° = h₁/24
1/√3 = h₁/24
h₁ = 24/√3 = 8√3 m

STEP 5: [Student to complete] Calculate the total height of the tower. Remember to add the observer's height.

Solution : Here, AB is the chimney, CD the observer and ∠ ADE the angle of elevation (see Fig. 9.6). In this case, ADE is a triangle, right-angled at E and we are required to find the height of the chimney.

We have AB = AE + BE = AE + 1.5
and DE = CB = 28.5 m

To determine AE, we choose a trigonometric ratio, which involves both AE and DE. Let us choose the tangent of the angle of elevation.

Now, tan 45° = AE/DE

concept_bullets: When the observer is elevated above the ground, the right triangle spans from eye level to the top of the structure, not from the ground. AE is the height above eye level; total height = AE + observer height.
For tan 45° = 1, the opposite side equals the adjacent side. So AE = DE = 28.5 m - a useful consistency check when the angle is 45°.
Total chimney height requires two-part decomposition: AB = AE + BE = AE + observer height = 28.5 + 1.5 = 30 m. Omitting BE gives a 5% underestimate.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: Example 3 introduces the observer eye-level offset: the observer CD is 1.5 m tall, standing 28.5 m from a chimney. The angle of elevation of the chimney top from the observer's eye (at D) is 45°. The right triangle is formed between the observer's eye (D) and the chimney top (A), not between the ground and the chimney top. Thus AE (the chimney height above eye level) is found by tan 45° = AE/DE: 1 = AE/28.5, giving AE = 28.5 m. The total chimney height is then AB = AE + BE = 28.5 + 1.5 = 30 m. The self-consistency check uses the fact that tan 45° = 1 requires AE = DE, which is confirmed since AE = DE = 28.5 m. The most common error - reporting AE = 28.5 m as the final answer without adding 1.5 m - is explicitly flagged.

We have AB = AE + BE = AE + 1.5
and DE = CB = 28.5 m

tan 45° = AE/DE

i.e., 1 = AE/28.5

Therefore, AE = 28.5

So the height of the chimney (AB) = (28.5 + 1.5) m = 30 m

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 - Diagram: Observer CD (eye at D, 1.5 m above ground). Chimney AB (A = top, B = base). Right triangle ADE: right angle at E, where E is the point on the chimney at eye level. DE = CB = 28.5 m (horizontal distance, adjacent to θ = 45°). AE = h₁ (height of chimney above eye level, unknown). AB = h₁ + 1.5 m (total height). Step 2 - Known: DE = 28.5 m, θ = 45°. Unknown: AE = h₁, then AB = h₁ + 1.5. Step 3 - Ratio: Adjacent = DE (known), opposite = AE (unknown). Use tan θ = AE / DE. Step 4 - Set up: tan 45° = AE / 28.5 → 1 = AE / 28.5 → AE = 28.5 m. Step 5 - Total height: AB = AE + BE = 28.5 + 1.5 = 30 m. The total height of the chimney is 30 m. Check: tan 45° = 28.5 / 28.5 = 1. Correct.
recall_questions.prompt: An observer 1.5 m tall stands 28.5 m from a chimney and measures the angle of elevation of the top of the chimney from her eyes as 45°. Calculate the total height of the chimney. Show all working including the decomposition of the total height into two parts.

recall_questions.answer: In observer-offset problems, the angle of elevation is measured from the observer's eye level (height CD above the ground), not from the ground. The right triangle used to find the height is formed between the observer's eye D and the top of the structure A, using the horizontal at eye level DE. This triangle yields AE - the height of the structure above the observer's eye level. The portion of the structure below the observer's eye level (BE = CD = observer's height) is not part of the computed height AE. Therefore: Total height of structure = AE + BE = (height above eye level) + (observer's own height). If BE is omitted, the answer is AE alone, which is smaller than the true total height by exactly the observer's height. In the example, AE = 28.5 m but the correct total height AB = 28.5 + 1.5 = 30 m. The general formula is: Total height = (trig ratio result) + (observer's eye-level height above ground).

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
APPLICATION

HOOK

During Uttarayan, the kite festival celebrated across Gujarat - particularly in Ahmedabad - thousands of kites fill the sky. Kavya is flying her kite on a rooftop terrace. The kite string is 80 m long and makes an angle of 30° with the ground. She wants to know how high the kite is above the rooftop. She knows the string length and the angle - but which quantity is the unknown, and which trigonometric ratio should she use? This section trains you to approach exactly such unfamiliar real-world problems using a structured translation method.

The problems in Exercise 9.1 (Q1-Q5) of the textbook - Section 9.1, pp. 141-142 - require you to translate a word problem into a right-triangle diagram, select the correct ratio, and solve. The following scaffolding shows you how to do this systematically.

TRANSLATION SCAFFOLDING

For every application problem involving a single angle of elevation, follow these six stages:

Stage 1 - Problem: Read the full problem statement carefully. Identify all numbers, all geometric objects (pole, rope, tree, kite), and the quantity being asked for.

Stage 2 - Situation (What is given?): Write a brief description of the physical situation in your own words. Identify the right triangle involved and state what forms the three sides.

Stage 3 - Known quantities: List every number given in the problem and assign variable labels. Use h for heights, d for horizontal distances, θ for angles.

Stage 4 - Unknown quantity: State exactly what you must find. Label it clearly (e.g., h = height of pole, d = length of string).

Stage 5 - Translate to equation: Write a trigonometric equation connecting the known and unknown quantities. Justify why you chose that particular ratio (opposite/adjacent → tan; opposite/hypotenuse → sin; adjacent/hypotenuse → cos).

Stage 6 - Solve and Check: Solve the equation algebraically, then verify that the numerical answer is physically reasonable given the geometry of the problem.

WORKED APPLICATION: Q1 from Exercise 9.1

Problem (Q1): A circus artist is climbing a 20 m long rope, which is tightly stretched and tied from the top of a vertical pole to the ground. Find the height of the pole, if the angle made by the rope with the ground level is 30° (see Fig. 9.11).

Stage 1 - Problem: A rope of length 20 m connects the top of a vertical pole to a point on the ground. The rope makes a 30° angle with the ground. Find the pole's height.

Stage 2 - Situation: The rope is the hypotenuse (slant line from ground point to top of pole). The pole is the vertical side (opposite to the 30° angle at the ground). The ground segment from the pole's foot to the rope's foot is the horizontal side (adjacent to the 30° angle). The right angle is at the base of the pole.

Stage 3 - Known quantities:
- Length of rope = 20 m (hypotenuse)
- θ = 30° (angle between rope and ground level)

Stage 4 - Unknown quantity:
- h = height of pole (opposite side to θ)

Stage 5 - Translate to equation:
Since the known side is the hypotenuse and the unknown side is the opposite side:
sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse
sin 30° = h / 20

WHY THIS STEP? You use sin (not tan) because the known quantity is the hypotenuse (rope length = 20 m) and the unknown quantity is the opposite side (pole height). If you used tan, you would introduce the adjacent side (ground distance) as a second unknown, making the problem unsolvable in one step.

Stage 6 - Solve and Check:
sin 30° = h/20
1/2 = h/20
h = 10 m

CHECK: Does the answer make physical sense? With an angle of only 30° and a rope of 20 m, the pole should be noticeably shorter than the rope. h = 10 m is exactly half the rope length, which matches sin 30° = 1/2. The ground distance would be 20 cos 30° = 20 × (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m. Verification using Pythagoras: h² + d² = 10² + (10√3)² = 100 + 300 = 400 = 20². Confirmed.

WORKED APPLICATION: Q5 from Exercise 9.1 (Kite-Flying Context)

Problem (Q5): A kite is flying at a height of 60 m above the ground. The string attached to the kite is temporarily tied to a point on the ground. The inclination of the string with the ground is 60°. Find the length of the string, assuming that there is no slack in the string.

Stage 1 - Problem: A kite is at 60 m height. The string makes 60° with the ground. Find the string length.

Stage 2 - Situation: The kite string is the hypotenuse (slant from ground tie-point to the kite). The height of the kite (60 m) is the vertical side (opposite to the 60° angle at the ground). The horizontal ground distance is the adjacent side.

Stage 3 - Known quantities:
- h = 60 m (height of kite = opposite side)
- θ = 60° (inclination of string with ground)

Stage 4 - Unknown quantity:
- String length = hypotenuse (call it L)

Stage 5 - Translate to equation:
Since the known side is the opposite side and the unknown is the hypotenuse:
sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse
sin 60° = 60 / L

Stage 6 - Solve and Check:
sin 60° = 60/L
√3/2 = 60/L
L = 60 × 2/√3 = 120/√3 = 40√3 m

CHECK: Does the answer make physical sense? With a 60° angle and a height of 60 m, the string is steeper than 45°, so the string length should be somewhat larger than the height. L = 40√3 ≈ 69.28 m is larger than 60 m, which is geometrically consistent with a steep inclination. Verification: L × sin 60° = 40√3 × (√3/2) = 40 × 3/2 = 60 m. Confirmed.

ERROR ALERT

A common and significant error in application problems is to place the angle of elevation at the wrong vertex of the triangle. For example, in Q1 above, the 30° angle is at the ground point where the rope meets the ground - not at the base of the pole, and not at the top of the pole. If you place the angle at the wrong vertex, every side label (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) reverses, and the equation you write will give an incorrect answer. Before writing any equation, confirm: at which vertex is the given angle θ located? Label that vertex, then identify opposite and adjacent sides relative to that specific vertex.

A second common error is to confuse the given angle with its complement. An angle of elevation of 30° is not the same as 60°; sin 30° ≠ sin 60°. Always substitute the given angle, not its complement.

CHECK - Self-Assessment for Q2, Q3, Q4 from Exercise 9.1

Use the six-stage translation scaffolding to attempt Q2, Q3, and Q4 from Exercise 9.1 (Section 9.1, pp. 141-142) independently. For each problem: (a) draw and label the right triangle, (b) list known and unknown quantities using h, d, θ, (c) identify the correct trig ratio with justification, (d) write and solve the equation, and (e) verify the answer is physically reasonable.

EXERCISE 9.1

1. A circus artist is climbing a 20 m long rope, which is tightly stretched and tied from the top of a vertical pole to the ground. Find the height of the pole, if the angle made by the rope with the ground level is 30° (see Fig. 9.11).

2. A tree breaks due to storm and the broken part bends so that the top of the tree touches the ground making an angle 30° with it. The distance between the foot of the tree to the point where the top touches the ground is 8 m. Find the height of the tree.

3. A contractor plans to install two slides for the children to play in a park. For the children below the age of 5 years, she prefers to have a slide whose top is at a height of 1.5 m, and is inclined at an angle of 30° to the ground, whereas for elder children, she wants to have a steep slide at a height of 3m, and inclined at an angle of 60° to the ground. What should be the length of the slide in each case?

4. The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point on the ground, which is 30 m away from the foot of the tower, is 30°. Find the height of the tower.

5. A kite is flying at a height of 60 m above the ground. The string attached to the kite is temporarily tied to a point on the ground. The inclination of the string with the ground is 60°. Find the length of the string, assuming that there is no slack in the string.
concept_bullets: When the rope or string is the hypotenuse and height is unknown, use sin θ = h/hypotenuse. For 20 m rope at 30°: h = 20 × sin 30° = 20 × (1/2) = 10 m.
Place the given angle at the correct vertex - the angle is formed at the ground point where rope meets ground, not at the pole base. Misplacing θ reverses opposite and adjacent labels.
Always verify with Pythagoras: for Q1, h² + d² = 10² + (10√3)² = 100 + 300 = 400 = 20². Confirmed.
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: This application topic trains students to independently translate word problems into right-triangle equations using a six-stage framework: Problem → Situation → Known quantities → Unknown quantity → Translate to equation → Solve and check. Applied to Q1 (circus artist climbing a 20 m rope at 30° to the ground), students identify the rope as the hypotenuse, the pole height as the opposite side, and select sin 30° = h/20, giving h = 10 m, verified using Pythagoras. Applied to Q5 (kite at 60 m height, string at 60° inclination), students identify height as the opposite side and string length as the hypotenuse, selecting sin 60° = 60/L, giving L = 40√3 m. A critical error - placing the given angle at the wrong vertex - reverses all side labels and produces incorrect equations. Students then attempt Q2-Q4 independently using the six-stage scaffolding.
important_points: A circus artist is climbing a 20 m long rope, which is tightly stretched and tied from the top of a vertical pole to the ground. Find the height of the pole, if the angle made by the rope with the ground level is 30°

A kite is flying at a height of 60 m above the ground. The string attached to the kite is temporarily tied to a point on the ground. The inclination of the string with the ground is 60°. Find the length of the string, assuming that there is no slack in the string.

recall_questions.answer: Stage 1 - Problem: Rope = 20 m (hypotenuse), angle with ground = 30°, find pole height. Stage 2 - Situation: The rope is the hypotenuse; the pole is the vertical side (opposite to 30° at the ground point); the horizontal ground distance is the adjacent side. Right angle at the base of the pole. Stage 3 - Known: Rope = hypotenuse = 20 m; θ = 30°. Stage 4 - Unknown: h = pole height (opposite to θ). Stage 5 - Translation: Known side is hypotenuse; unknown is opposite. Use sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse. sin 30° = h / 20. Stage 6 - Solve: 1/2 = h / 20 → h = 10 m. Check: ground distance = 20 cos 30° = 20 × √3/2 = 10√3 m. Pythagoras: 10² + (10√3)² = 100 + 300 = 400 = 20². Confirmed. The height of the pole is 10 m.
recall_questions.prompt: A circus artist climbs a rope 20 m long tied from the top of a vertical pole to the ground. The rope makes a 30° angle with the ground. Using a labelled diagram and the six-stage translation method, formulate the right-triangle equation and calculate the height of the pole.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 - Diagram: Right triangle. Ground tie-point at C, kite at A (60 m above ground), point B directly below A on the ground (right angle at B). θ = ∠ACB = 60° (angle of inclination). AB = 60 m (opposite), BC = horizontal distance (adjacent), CA = L = string length (hypotenuse, unknown). Step 2 - Known: AB = 60 m (opposite), θ = 60°. Unknown: CA = L (hypotenuse). Step 3 - Ratio: Known side is opposite; unknown is hypotenuse. Use sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse → sin 60° = 60 / L. Step 4 - Substitute sin 60° = √3/2: √3/2 = 60/L → L = 120/√3 = 40√3 m. Check: L × sin 60° = 40√3 × √3/2 = 40 × 3/2 = 60 m. Confirmed. The length of the string is 40√3 m (approximately 69.3 m).
